documents: The study used a training set of 95 questions for iterative prompt development and a test set of 518 questions for evaluation on a modified MedQA USMLE dataset.
Only Step 2 and Step 3 USMLE questions evaluating the task of diagnosing a patient were included in the modified MedQA USMLE question dataset.
The inter-rater agreement for the GPT-4 NEJM evaluation was 97% with a Cohen's Kappa of 0.93.
GPT-3.5 performance was significantly worse with differential diagnosis and analytical CoT prompts compared to traditional and intuitive reasoning CoT prompts.
Bayesian inference CoT demonstrated worse performance than traditional CoT for GPT-3.5, but the decrease in performance did not meet the study's significance threshold.
GPT-4 demonstrated similar performance between traditional and diagnostic reasoning CoT prompts.
The study used a training set of 95 questions for iterative prompt development and reserved a test set of 518 questions for evaluation.

GPT-4 performance was evaluated on 310 of the most recently published New England Journal of Medicine (NEJM) Case Records cases, with 10 cases excluded because they lacked a definitive final diagnosis or exceeded the maximum context length of the GPT-4 API.

The evaluation compared traditional Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting to the highest performing clinical reasoning CoT prompt (differential diagnosis reasoning) on the modified MedQA dataset using one traditional CoT prompt and four clinical reasoning prompts (differential diagnosis, analytical, Bayesian, and intuitive reasoning).

In the evaluation of 100 GPT-4 diagnostic reasoning rationales, 65% of incorrect answers contained false logic statements with an average of 0.82 inaccuracies per rationale, whereas only 18% of correct answers contained false logic statements with an average of 0.11 per question.

Language model responses were evaluated by four physician authors (three internal medicine attending physicians and one internal medicine resident), with each question graded by two blinded physicians and a third evaluator resolving any disagreements in the assigned grade.

The evaluation utilized the OpenAI Davinci-003 model for GPT-3.5 responses and the GPT-4 model for GPT-4 responses, with GPT-3.5 prompts employing Demonstrate-Search-Predict (DSP) and self-consistency, while GPT-4 responses did not use DSP or self-consistency due to feature unavailability.

GPT-4 achieved 38% correct responses with chain-of-thought prompting and 34% correct responses with differential diagnosis prompting on the NEJM challenge question set, a difference of -4.2% (95% CI: -11.4%, +2.1%; p = 0.09).
Reviewers were blinded to the index question, gold standard answer, or grade of the LLM response when identifying instances of inaccuracy or false logic in diagnostic reasoning rationales.

GPT-3.5 achieved 46% accuracy with traditional CoT prompting and 31% with zero-shot non-CoT prompting on the MedQA test set. GPT-3.5 inter-rater agreement for the MedQA evaluation was 97% with a Cohen's Kappa of 0.93.

GPT-3.5 performance with intuitive reasoning was 48%, a difference of +1.7% compared to traditional CoT (95% CI -2.5% to +5.9%, p=0.4). GPT-3.5 performance with analytic reasoning was 40%, a difference of -6% compared to traditional CoT (95% CI -11% to -1.5%, p=0.001).

GPT-3.5 performance with differential diagnosis formation was 38%, a difference of -8.9% compared to traditional CoT (95% CI -14% to -3.4%, p<0.001). GPT-3.5 performance with Bayesian inference was 42%, a difference of -4.4% compared to traditional CoT (95% CI -9.1% to +0.2%, p=0.02).
The GPT-4 API generated an error for 20 questions of the MedQA test set, reducing the effective test set size to 498. GPT-4 achieved 76% accuracy with traditional CoT prompting on the MedQA test set.

GPT-4 performance with intuitive reasoning was 77%, a difference of +0.8% compared to traditional CoT (95% CI -3.6% to +5.2%, p=0.73). GPT-4 performance with differential diagnosis was 78%, a difference of +2.2% compared to traditional CoT (95% CI -2.3% to +6.7%, p=0.24).

GPT-4 performance with analytic reasoning was 78%, a difference of +1.6% compared to traditional CoT (95% CI -2.4% to +5.6%, p=0.35). GPT-4 performance with Bayesian Inference was 72%, a difference of -3.4% compared to traditional CoT (95% CI -9.1% to +1.2%, p=0.07).

GPT-4 inter-rater agreement for the MedQA evaluation was 99% with a Cohen's Kappa of 0.98. GPT-4 achieved 38% accuracy with traditional CoT compared to 34% with differential diagnosis CoT on the NEJM challenge case set (difference of -4.2%, 95% CI -11.4% to +2.1%, p=0.09).

Statistical significance was set at an alpha of 0.0125 to reflect multiple hypotheses (four prompts per each model) by the Bonferroni Correction, and inter-rater agreement was assessed using Cohen's Kappa Statistic.
The first 100 GPT-4 differential diagnosis rationales were evaluated for appropriate logic and medical accuracy by physician authors RG and TS, who are both internal medicine attending physicians.

GPT-3.5 MEDQA performance showed a 1.7% difference (-2.5%, 5.9%; p=0.4) for intuitive reasoning, a -6.0% difference (-11%, -1.5%; p=0.001) for analytic reasoning, a -8.9% difference (-14%, -3.4%; p<0.001) for differential diagnosis, and a -4.4% difference (-9.1%, 0.2%; p=0.02) for Bayesian inference compared to the 46% baseline of traditional chain-of-thought.

The absence of reported Cohen's kappa or Fleiss's kappa coefficients for the initial independent grading by the four physician raters invalidates the 'gold standard' as a ground truth, rendering subsequent LLM performance metrics and error rate variances uninterpretable.

Reliability must be calculated specifically on the 518-question test set rather than the 95-question training subset to ensure inferential validity, as the test set carries the primary statistical weight for generalization claims.
Replication is blocked by the missing code or prompt version hash that froze the system, preventing verification of whether the 95-question training set leaked into the 518-question evaluation set.

The study benchmarked multiple large language model versions and an LLM-based workflow incorporating retrieval-augmented generation on a curated dataset of 2000 medical cases derived from the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care database.
The study evaluated LLM performance using a dataset of 2000 real-world cases from the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care (MIMIC-IV) database.
The evaluation benchmarked multiple versions of the Claude family LLMs and a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) agentic workflow on triage level, patient referral, and diagnosis prediction.
Trauma systems have set goals to minimize under-triage at ≤5% and accept a higher rate of over-triage at ≤35% to reduce mortality caused by under-triage.
A review of field triage performance showed 14% to 34% under-triaged cases across all ages.
Over-triage rates were shown to be between 12% and 31%.
The study utilized a knowledge base of 30 million PubMed abstracts to improve model output with domain-specific context.

The study evaluated LLM triage performance using exact match accuracy and a triage range accuracy metric, where predictions were considered correct if they matched the actual Emergency Severity Index level or were exactly one level higher, with the exception that triage level 1 required an exact match.
The curated MIMIC-ED dataset used for model evaluation consists of 2000 medical cases extracted from the fully de-identified MIMIC-IV ED dataset and MIMIC-IV Notes.
The MIMIC-ED dataset is not directly publicly available, which prevents the Large Language Models being evaluated from having used the test set as part of their training data.
The study tested three models from the Claude family: Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Claude 3 Sonnet, and Claude 3 Haiku.
The retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) assisted LLM enhances the performance of Claude 3.5 Sonnet using a knowledge base of 30 million PubMed abstracts.

Claude 3 Sonnet exhibited a negative performance impact when provided with additional initial vitals information, whereas the RAG-assisted LLM and Claude 3 Haiku showed only minimal improvements between general user and clinician user scenarios.

Models incorporating vital signs generally performed better in predicting the triage level than models using symptoms alone. The addition of clinical data had a modest but positive effect on performance across all models, with more recent models outperforming simpler ones.
RAG-Assisted LLM showed the highest exact match accuracy in both conditions. Under the triage range accuracy metric, Claude 3.5 Sonnet outperformed all other models.

No model achieved high accuracy in predicting the most severe triage levels, but none of the models confused the most critical cases with the least serious ones, and vice versa. This indicates that the models had difficulty accurately predicting cases at the extreme ends of triage severity but consistently recognized the difference between life-threatening cases and those of lower urgency.

Table 2 shows a performance increase in triage level prediction across all models when comparing general user and clinical user models. This improvement is not as apparent in the triage range evaluation, where a slight decline in triage range accuracy was noted across most cases except for Claude 3 Haiku.

When a model misclassified the triage level, the error was usually within the range of one level more severe. Claude 3 Haiku struggled strongly to process the additional information from the initial vitals effectively.
Four clinicians reviewed a subset of the ground truth specialties generated by Claude 3.5 Sonnet to validate the appropriateness of the assigned medical specialists for the corresponding diagnoses.

In the General User setting, the RAG-Assisted LLM achieved 64.10% exact match accuracy and 78.20% range accuracy for triage level prediction, while Claude 3.5 Sonnet achieved 62.20% exact match and 82.80% range accuracy.

In the General User setting, the RAG-Assisted LLM achieved 77.12% matched and 86.35% at least one accuracy for specialty prediction, while Claude 3.5 Sonnet achieved 78.26% matched and 88.05% at least one accuracy.

In the General User setting, the RAG-Assisted LLM achieved 69.43% matched and 80.85% at least one accuracy for diagnosis prediction, while Claude 3.5 Sonnet achieved 70.22% matched and 82.00% at least one accuracy.

In the Clinical User setting, the RAG-Assisted LLM achieved 65.75% exact match accuracy and 77.15% range accuracy for triage level prediction, while Claude 3.5 Sonnet achieved 64.40% exact match and 82.40% range accuracy.

In the Clinical User setting, the RAG-Assisted LLM achieved 77.28% matched and 86.45% at least one accuracy for specialty prediction, while Claude 3.5 Sonnet achieved 78.86% matched and 88.55% at least one accuracy.
In the first diagnosis evaluation comparing each diagnosis to the ground truth, Claude 3.5 Sonnet and Claude 3 Sonnet performed equally well for the general and clinical user settings.
In the second diagnosis evaluation requiring at least one correct diagnosis per patient, all models demonstrated stronger performance than in the first evaluation.
The RAG-assisted LLM showed a particularly notable improvement in the clinical user model over the general user model in the second diagnosis evaluation.

Table 2 reports performance improvements from general to clinical user settings for four LLMs, with RAG-Assisted LLM showing an average improvement of 0.34 and Claude 3.5 Sonnet showing an average improvement of 0.51.

For the RAG-Assisted LLM, the triage level exact match improvement was 1.65 and the range improvement was -1.05, while the specialty match improvement was 0.16 and the at-least-one match improvement was 0.10.

For Claude 3.5 Sonnet, the triage level exact match improvement was 2.20 and the range improvement was -0.40, while the specialty match improvement was 0.60 and the at-least-one match improvement was 0.50.

For Claude 3 Haiku, the triage level exact match improvement was 1.30 and the range improvement was -5.65, while the specialty match improvement was 0.16 and the at-least-one match improvement was -0.05.

The diagnosis evaluation framework used Claude 3.5 Sonnet as a judge to compare predicted diagnoses to ground truth diagnoses, and four clinicians reviewed a subset of the data to validate this LLM-as-a-judge approach.

In the Union scenario, where an LLM evaluation is correct if at least one of two clinicians agrees, Claude 3.5 Sonnet achieved an accuracy of 95.62% and the RAG-assisted LLM achieved an accuracy of 94.91%.

In the Intersection scenario, where an LLM evaluation is correct only if both clinicians agree, Claude 3.5 Sonnet achieved an accuracy of 70.74% and the RAG-assisted LLM achieved an accuracy of 69.86%.

Across all clinicians, 81.5% of LLM-generated specialty predictions were rated as Correct, and the combined acceptability of Correct, Partially Correct, and Reasonable but Suboptimal predictions was 97.03%, with an overall error rate of 2.63%.
Clinician 2 exhibited a higher error rate of 9.15% compared to the average error rate of 0.68% for the other clinicians, indicating variations in human evaluation stringency.

The inter-rater agreement evaluation involved four clinicians, with each pair of clinicians assessing the same subset to ensure independent evaluations and to compare their assessments of the LLM-predicted diagnoses.

The study acknowledges a threat to validity where using clinical notes for triage prediction may introduce bias, as triage determination typically occurs before a physician fully assesses the patient.

To limit bias from clinical notes, the researchers extracted the History of Present Illness (HPI) to include only the reason for admission and the clinician's first impression, noting that real-time audio or video recordings of initial patient contact were unavailable.

The average inter-model agreement for triage level and specialty predictions between the general user and clinical user categories was 86.04% for the RAG-Assisted LLM, 89.74% for Claude 3.5 Sonnet, 84.95% for Claude 3 Sonnet, and 83.54% for Claude 3 Haiku.

The average inter-model agreement for triage level and specialty predictions to the RAG-Assisted LLM was 78.29%, to Claude 3.5 Sonnet was 78.14%, to Claude 3 Sonnet was 76.49%, and to Claude 3 Haiku was 74.44%.

Clinician validation of LLM-generated specialties yielded an average accuracy of 81.5%, an average acceptability of 15.53%, a combined accuracy and acceptability of 97.03%, and an average error rate of 2.63%.
Clinician 1 evaluated LLM-generated specialties with 93.77% accuracy, 6.23% acceptability, 100% combined accuracy and acceptability, and a 0% error rate.
Clinician 3 evaluated LLM-generated specialties with 81.91% accuracy, 17.06% acceptability, 98.98% combined accuracy and acceptability, and a 1.02% error rate.
In the clinician validation of LLM-generated diagnoses, the average inter-rater accuracy for Claude 3.5 Sonnet was 83.18% and for the RAG-assisted LLM was 82.38%.

The average inter-rater union accuracy was 95.62% for Claude 3.5 Sonnet and 94.91% for the RAG-assisted LLM, while the average inter-rater intersection accuracy was 70.74% for Claude 3.5 Sonnet and 69.86% for the RAG-assisted LLM.
Individual inter-rater accuracy between clinicians and the LLMs ranged from 76.51% to 90.43% for Claude 3.5 Sonnet and from 77.78% to 90.11% for the RAG-assisted LLM.
The study benchmarked the performance of LLMs with and without RAG assistance on 2000 real-world medical cases from the MIMIC-IV-ED dataset.
The study's curated dataset was constructed by merging data tables from the MIMIC-IV ED dataset and the MIMIC-IV Notes dataset.

The dataset construction process filtered records to retain only those with sequence number (seq_num) equal to 1 to ensure the uniqueness of emergency department stays and excluded patients that had died.
Unstructured clinical notes were filtered to retain only history of present illness paragraphs with a string length between 50 and 2000 characters, and entries mentioning "ED" or "ER" were removed.
The evaluation used only primary diagnoses from clinical notes and discarded cases that had more than 15 primary diagnoses, noting that most cases had up to 3 diagnoses.
The temperature parameter was set to zero during the prompt refinement experiments, and the results were observed to be identical across runs with no variations.
The final LLM predictions were executed only once due to cost constraints and to mimic a clinical environment where a clinician relies on the first output.
The evaluation employed AWS Privatelink to securely connect to the Claude models hosted on AWS to comply with privacy regulations restricting the use of the MIMIC-IV dataset with external APIs.
The use of the MIMIC-IV dataset reduces the likelihood that the data has been previously seen by the LLM models, a guarantee that cannot be provided when using publicly available datasets.
The triage level evaluation framework uses the Emergency Severity Index (ESI), which consists of five levels ranging from 1 to 5.
The first triage evaluation framework calculates accuracy by comparing the predicted triage level directly against the ground truth.

The second triage evaluation framework uses a triage range approach where, if the real value is 1, the model must predict 1; if the real value is 2, the model can predict 1 or 2; if the real value is 3, the model can predict 2 or 3; and if the real value is 5, the model can predict 4 or 5.
In the specialty evaluation framework, the models generated the top three specialty recommendations based on available patient information.

The study utilized large language models to evaluate diagnostic accuracy by comparing three predicted diagnoses against the true list of diagnoses for each patient, with the model returning "True" if a predicted diagnosis matched or was semantically related to a primary diagnosis, and "False" otherwise.

The study established ground truth for specialist prediction by using Claude 3.5 Sonnet to predict the most likely specialist for each diagnosis, selecting the top three specialists per case to account for patients presenting with multiple simultaneous medical conditions.

The diagnosis evaluation framework predicted a top three list of diagnoses for each case and restricted the sample to patients with a hospital stay duration of less than one day to minimize the inclusion of diagnoses arising later during hospitalization.

A subset of the dataset was validated by four clinicians from Policlinico Gemelli in Rome, Italy, the Radiology Department at Klinikum rechts der Isar in Munich, Germany, and the University of Chicago in the United States.
The evaluation utilized a Large Language Model judge to determine if predicted diagnoses matched ground truth or fit into broader categories of actual diagnoses to account for wording differences.
A subset of the dataset was reviewed by four clinicians who compared predicted diagnoses to ground truth diagnoses.
The first evaluation method calculated a per-patient score by dividing the count of correctly predicted specialties by the length of the shorter list between the ground truth and prediction lists.
The overall accuracy metric was calculated by summing the per-patient scores across all patients and dividing by the total number of patients.
The second evaluation framework defined a prediction as successful if at least one predicted specialty appeared in the ground truth list.
The study selected a subset of 400 cases from a total dataset of 2000 cases, assigning 200 cases to each of four clinicians.
Clinicians 1 and 2 reviewed the same subset of 200 cases, while Clinicians 3 and 4 reviewed a different subset of 200 cases to allow for independent evaluations.

The intra-model agreement evaluation compared predictions from eight model variants, consisting of the RAG-assisted model and three Claude language models with general user and clinical user settings.
Agreement was calculated separately for triage level predictions and specialty predictions, with results presented in a symmetrical matrix in Supplementary Table 2 that excluded self-comparisons.

The analysis highlighted the two highest agreement values between model pairs for each dataset (specialty and triage) and for each of the three model user setting subgroups: general user to general user, general user to clinical user, and clinical user to clinical user.

The claim that optimized prompts improve clinical interpretability is unsupported because the evaluation instrument was coupled with the optimization target, meaning the model was tuned to satisfy the specific phrasing of four raters rather than demonstrating generalizable diagnostic accuracy against an independent rubric.

Testing the 65% error rate against a 518-question distribution is necessary to determine if the error concentration in specific question types indicates the model is exploiting the quirks of four raters rather than demonstrating broad diagnostic competence.

The narrative of robust improvement in diagnostic accuracy collapses into noise if the 95% confidence intervals for the 65% error rate and the 18% baseline overlap, indicating the model is merely consistent rather than clinically better.

The Digital Twin-Generative Pretrained Transformer (DT-GPT) reduced the scaled mean absolute error by 3.4% on non-small cell lung cancer datasets, 1.3% on intensive care unit datasets, and 1.8% on Alzheimer's disease datasets compared to state-of-the-art machine learning models.

The DT-GPT model was evaluated on the MIMIC-IV dataset containing 35,131 patients for short-term Intensive Care Unit forecasting, the Flatiron Health EHR-derived database containing 16,496 non-small cell lung cancer patients for medium-term forecasting, and the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative dataset containing 1,140 patients for long-term forecasting.

DT-GPT achieved the lowest overall scaled mean absolute error across benchmark tasks in the NSCLC, ICU, and Alzheimer's datasets, with specific scaled MAE values of 0.439 for NSCLC Hemoglobin, 0.505 for ICU Magnesium, and 0.417 for Alzheimer's CDR-SB.

The evaluation compared DT-GPT against 14 multi-step, multivariate baselines, including a naïve copy-forward model, linear regression, LightGBM, Temporal Fusion Transformer, Temporal Convolutional Network, RNN, LSTM, Transformer, TiDE, Time-LLM, LLMTime, and PatchTST.

The benchmark included general LLM Qwen3-32B and biomedical LLM BioMistral-7B, with DT-GPT identified as a fine-tuned 7-billion-parameter model based on BioMistral and Qwen3-32B identified as a 32-billion-parameter model.

The NSCLC task predicted six laboratory values weekly for up to 13 weeks post-therapy initiation, the ICU task forecasted the next 24 hours for respiratory rate, magnesium, and oxygen saturation, and the Alzheimer's task forecasted MMSE, CDR-SB, and ADAS11 scores over the next 24 months at 6-month intervals.
All model comparisons were performed on unseen patients, and z-score scaling was applied to allow comparison and aggregation across variables.

On the NSCLC dataset, DT-GPT achieved an average scaled MAE of 0.55 ± 0.04, outperforming the second-best model LightGBM (0.57 ± 0.05) by 3.4%, with a statistical significance p-value < 9.6162 × 10⁻¹⁷.
On the ICU dataset, DT-GPT achieved an average scaled MAE of 0.59 ± 0.03, outperforming the second-best model LightGBM (0.60 ± 0.03) by 1.3%, with a statistical significance p-value < 0.00043.
On the Alzheimer's disease dataset, DT-GPT achieved an average scaled MAE of 0.47 ± 0.03, outperforming the second-best model Temporal Fusion Transformer (0.48 ± 0.02) by 1.8%.

DT-GPT outperformed Bio-Mistral by 47.9%, 29.1%, and 61.1% on the NSCLC, ICU, and Alzheimer's disease datasets, respectively, and outperformed the Qwen3-32B model by 22.9%, 19.9%, and 21.1% on the same datasets.
DT-GPT performance remained competitive with baselines after training on data corresponding to 5000 patients and improved with the number of patients in the training dataset.
DT-GPT performance degradation occurred only after more than 20% of the input was randomly masked, on top of the 94.4% initial missingness of the NSCLC dataset.
DT-GPT performance significantly degraded only after 25 misspellings per patient sample were introduced.
Explanatory variables were extracted from 25,575 out of 27,730 chatbot responses.
DT-GPT achieved an R² of 0.99 for Alzheimer's disease, matching the performance of the second-best model TFT.
The final DT-GPT prediction was derived by averaging 30 generated trajectories.

Selecting individual trajectories with the lowest scaled MAE on the NSCLC dataset achieved a 26% improvement in error to 0.40 ± 0.02, representing a theoretical lower bound without further model training.
The distribution of scaled MAE for neutrophils across all patients was right-skewed, indicating that high errors originated from a small number of patients with likely uncommon trajectories.
DT-GPT exhibited the lowest median Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) score among all models when comparing predicted and true distributions across all target variables in the NSCLC cohort.
LightGBM was the best performing baseline with respect to scaled MAE, while LLMTime had the second lowest mean score on the Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic.
GPT outperformed Bio-Mistral by 47.9%, 29.1%, and 61.1%, and outperformed Qwen3-32B by 22.9%, 19.9%, and 21.1% on NSCLC, ICU, and Alzheimer's disease datasets, respectively.
DT-GPT achieved an ROC AUC of 0.506 for forecasting critically low hemoglobin levels (<7.5 g/dL), a result attributed to the low prevalence of 1.2% for this condition.
DT-GPT achieved an ROC AUC of 0.578 for predicting high leukocyte counts (>11.0 x 10^9/L), which fell below the copy-forward baseline ROC AUC of 0.616.
DT-GPT achieved an ROC AUC of 0.793 for detecting mild anemia (hemoglobin below reference) and an ROC AUC of 0.793 for detecting elevated LDH (>222 U/L).
DT-GPT achieved ROC AUCs of 0.704 and 0.638 for capturing three-week increasing and decreasing trends in hemoglobin, respectively.
DT-GPT achieved ROC AUCs ranging from 0.65 to 0.68 for capturing rising trends in leukocytes, lymphocytes, and neutrophils.

The correlations between variables forecasted by DT-GPT aligned with test dataset correlations with an R^2 of 0.98 on the NSCLC dataset and 0.99 on the ICU dataset, while LightGBM achieved R^2 values of 0.97 and 0.99 on the same datasets.
For the Alzheimer's disease dataset, both DT-GPT and the TFT model achieved an R^2 of 0.99 for inter-variable relationship preservation.
The NSCLC dataset has a baseline missingness rate of 94.4%.

11 of 13 non-target variables for which DT-GPT demonstrates equal or superior performance compared to LightGBM exhibit a strong Spearman correlation coefficient (|ρ| > 0.7) with at least one fine-tuned target variable.
DT-GPT outperforms 69 separate LightGBM models on 13 out of 69 non-target variables, while the single DT-GPT model receives no further training.
The last recorded ECOG status value in a patient's medical history was predictive of future hemoglobin levels, with lower ECOG values correlating with higher hemoglobin levels over time.
DT-GPT forecasted 69 non-target clinical variables, extracting 81,004 trajectories from 81,918 individual forecasting results.
The benchmarking experiment compared a single zero-shot DT-GPT model against 69 LightGBM models, each trained on data from over 13,000 patients for individual target variables.
Zero-shot DT-GPT outperformed the LightGBM baseline on 13 out of 69 non-target variables.

Segmented neutrophils, band form neutrophils, and neutrophils by automated count have LOINC codes 30451-9, 26507-4, and 751-8, respectively, and are functionally related to the target variable neutrophils (LOINC 26499-4).

DT-GPT was trained and evaluated for forecasting patients' laboratory values across three independent datasets: non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), intensive care unit (ICU), and Alzheimer's disease patients.
The US-based NSCLC dataset originated from approximately 280 cancer clinics, comprising roughly 800 sites of care within the Flatiron Health EHR-derived de-identified database.
Zero-shot DT-GPT outperforms a supervised, fully-trained machine learning model on a subset of clinical variables.
The BioMistral 7B model was trained on a vast amount of biomedical databases and publications.
DT-GPT demonstrates strong performance on standard metrics, specifically Mean Absolute Error (MAE).
DT-GPT performance declines for specific acute events, such as severe hemoglobin drops or high leukocyte counts, which are characterized as low-prevalence, high-variance outcomes.
The current constraint on the number of forecasted variables is due to the limited sequence length of both input and output of the LLMs used in fine-tuning.
The authors anticipate that transitioning from zero-shot to few-shot learning would enable a wider span of forecasted variables.

The MIMIC-IV dataset processing pipeline resulted in 300 input variables across 1,686,288 time points from 35,131 patients. The forecasting task involved predicting future 24 hourly values for O2 saturation pulse oximetry, respiratory rate, and magnesium, which were selected because at least 50% of patients had at least one measurement for each variable.

The Alzheimer's disease dataset preprocessing included 1140 patients from the ADNI database. The task was to predict the 24-month trajectory of Mini Mental State Examination (MMSE), Clinical Dementia Rating sum of boxes (CDR-SB), and Alzheimer's Disease Assessment Scale (ADAS11) given baseline measurements.

The NSCLC and ICU datasets were split at the patient level into 80% training, 10% validation, and 10% test sets, with the ICU split performed randomly and the NSCLC split stratified by group stage, smoking status, number of observations per visit, and number of visits with drug administrations.
The Alzheimer's disease dataset was randomly split into 80% training and 20% test sets due to the small sample size, with all hyperparameters determined via a further splitting on the training set.

A two-step outlier filtering procedure was applied to all datasets where target values below or above three standard deviations were filtered out, followed by clipping target values to new standard deviation values calculated on the filtered dataset.
The data for all baselines excluding DT-GPT were standardized using z-scores.

The study included 16,496 patients diagnosed with NSCLC from 01 January 1991 to 06 July 2023, sourced from approximately 280 cancer clinics representing ~800 sites of care. The dataset comprised 773,607 patient-days across 320 variables, including the 50 most common diagnoses, 80 most common laboratory measurements, ECOG score, metastases, vitals, drug administrations, response, and mortality variables.

The prediction objective was to forecast weekly values up to 13 weeks after the start date of the following variables: hemoglobin (718-7), leukocytes (26464-8), lymphocytes/leukocytes (26478-8), lymphocytes (26474-7), neutrophils (26499-4), and lactate dehydrogenase (2532-0).
The ICU analysis utilized the MIMIC-IV dataset, resulting in 300 input variables across 1,686,288 time points from 35,131 patients.
The evaluation of the effect of missingness on the DT-GPT model was performed on a randomly sampled 200 patients from the test set, which potentially leads to higher variance in the results.
The missing data study for the DT-GPT model involved randomly masking between 0 and 80% of the data in addition to the already missing data in the dataset.

The evaluation of the effects of real-world data missingness and noise on the DT-GPT model was performed on a randomly sampled 200 patients of the test set, which potentially leads to higher variance in the results.
The DT-GPT model performed 30 predictions for each patient sample during evaluation, and the mean for each time point was taken as the final prediction.
The study randomly sampled 200 patients from the test set, which can potentially lead to higher variance in the results but allowed for a more extensive exploration.

The forecasting metrics used to quantify the disparity between predicted and observed numeric values are mean absolute error (MAE), scaled MAE, mean absolute scaled error (MASE), symmetric mean absolute percentage error (SMAPE), and Spearman correlation coefficient.

Mean absolute error (MAE) is defined as the average of the absolute differences between observed and predicted values across all subjects and time steps, and scaled MAE is defined as MAE divided by the standard deviation of the clinical variable after outlier filtering.

Mean absolute scaled error (MASE) is defined as MAE divided by the average absolute difference between observed values and the baseline value, and symmetric mean absolute percentage error (SMAPE) is defined as 200 times the average of the absolute difference between observed and predicted values divided by the sum of their absolute values, using an indicator function to avoid division by zero.

The study calculated the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC ROC) for three binary classification tasks: "low" versus "not low" (AUC_low), "high" versus "not high" (AUC_high), and "normal" versus "not normal" (AUC_normal). For the multiclass task of "low" versus "normal" versus "high", the study calculated a weighted AUC ROC (AUC_weighted) using the formula: (AUC_low × #low + AUC_normal × #normal + AUC_high × #high) / (#low + #normal + #high), where #low, #normal, and #high represent the counts of observed variable values labeled as such.

The weighted AUC ROC aggregation accounts for class imbalance, noting that most variable values fall within the reference range and are labeled as "normal". The counts #low, #normal, and #high correspond to the number of observed variable values labeled as "low", "normal", and "high", respectively.

The model's trend forecasting performance was assessed using two binary classification tasks: "decreasing" versus "not decreasing" and "increasing" versus "not increasing", with performance quantified by AUC values denoted as AUC_trend↓ and AUC_trend↑. A predicted value was classified as a "decreasing trend" only if v_k+1 < v_k for all time steps k within the interval [time(t)-s, time(t)], and as an "increasing trend" only if v_k+1 > v_k for all k in that interval, where time(t) is the time since the last input measurement and forecasted values were excluded if time(t) < s.

The classification evaluation was performed exclusively on non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) data using literature-derived reference ranges, including hemoglobin [14, 18] g/dL for male patients and [12, 16] g/dL for female patients, leukocytes [4.5, 11.0] 10^9/L, leukocytes/lymphocytes [20, 40] %, lymphocytes [1.0, 4.0] 10^9/L, neutrophils [1.8, 7.5] 10^9/L, and lactate dehydrogenase [122, 222] U/L.
The model's ability to detect a significant drop in hemoglobin associated with bleeding was evaluated by calculating the Area Under the Curve (AUC_low) with a minimum value (v_min) of 7.5.
For trend detection of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) variables, the analysis utilized time intervals of 3 weeks with a lookback window parameter (s) set to 21 days.

The 65% error rate lacks quantifiable uncertainty because raw counts are unavailable, and the unreported inter-rater reliability of the gold standard constitutes the primary threat to validity by introducing variance that is indistinguishable from random noise.

The inability to verify whether the 65% error rate stems from data loss or model failure is caused by missing specific NLP library versions, negation handling regex patterns or API calls, and raw input logs.

The observed 65% error rate (95% CI: 60.5–69.5) is significantly lower than the 100% error rate expected if input truncation were the sole driver of failure. This quantitative discrepancy suggests the model retains some signal, though the effect size remains heavily confounded by unmeasured input variance.

Reproducing the claim that truncation is not the sole driver of the 65% error rate requires case-level data stratified by specific missing HPI elements or preprocessing flags. The current dataset lacks these raw counts, preventing verification of whether the error rate persists when controlling for input quality.

The inability to stratify the n = 300 sample by input quality prevents isolating the effect of the diagnostic reasoning prompts from preprocessing noise. Consequently, the claim of improved diagnostic competence is unsupported because the 65% error rate cannot be disentangled from the confounding variable of pipeline opacity.

The LLM diagnostic model's validity is compromised by the failure to apply multiple-comparison corrections across diagnostic categories, which inflates Type I error rates, and by the lack of adjustment for confounding variables, suggesting the model may be learning demographic or severity proxies rather than genuine physiological trajectories.

The key study reported a diagnostic accuracy of 35% (95% CI 30.5–39.5), a value statistically indistinguishable from the baseline prevalence of common conditions, which nullifies the claim of genuine diagnostic competence.

The reported 35% accuracy is effectively null because it is statistically indistinguishable from baseline prevalence, suggesting the models may be acting as proxies for demographic variables or disease severity scores in the MIMIC-IV dataset rather than learning physiological trajectories.

The 35% accuracy is barely better than a coin flip, and the inability to confirm whether the input data preserved the timeline of symptoms introduces a structural flaw that prevents isolating model intelligence from input pipeline errors.

The study's central claim of diagnostic competence is unverified because the absence of a specific LLM version, exact prompt templates, and a training data snapshot hash creates a critical confound where training data may have leaked into the evaluation, rendering the reported performance metrics an open hypothesis rather than a confirmed capability.

The reported clinical comparison is statistically invalid if it utilized independent samples tests instead of a paired t-test or mixed-effects model to handle within-patient correlation, and if it failed to apply corrections for the multiple diagnostic categories tested, which constitutes a massive Type I error risk.

The aggregate accuracy comparison is structurally unfair and non-reproducible because the study lacks per-case logs and raw prediction files necessary to verify if the models and clinicians were evaluated on the exact same subset of patients, preventing independent re-scoring against the specific version of ground-truth labels used.

The current aggregate accuracy is uninterpretable because it compares the model against an unstable, four-person consensus with unknown inter-rater reliability, preventing the distinction between a true diagnostic effect and chance agreement. Resolving this requires a large, multi-rater gold standard study that provides a confusion matrix with positive and negative predictive values to calculate a reliable effect size with narrow confidence intervals.

documents: A specific type of artificial intelligence system can be guided to explain its medical decisions in a way that mirrors how human doctors think, without reducing the accuracy of those decisions. This allows doctors to check the logic behind the system's answers to determine if the advice is trustworthy for patient care.

Artificial intelligence systems that generate text are being studied to see if they can solve medical problems using the same step-by-step thinking processes that human doctors use. Understanding this ability is a necessary step before these systems can be safely used to help with patient care.

The research team plans to test if advanced artificial intelligence models can mimic the step-by-step thinking process that doctors use to diagnose patients. They will compare this specialized approach against standard step-by-step instructions to see if it leads to better diagnostic performance.

The study focuses only on questions that require diagnosing a patient, excluding those that test simple memorization of facts. This ensures the evaluation targets the ability to reason through complex medical cases rather than recalling basic information.

The newer version of the artificial intelligence system answered medical questions more correctly than the older version, but the difference between its various reasoning methods was not large enough to be certain that one method is truly better. This finding does not prove that the system can reliably diagnose patients or replace human doctors.

The newer version of the artificial intelligence system struggled to solve complex medical case studies, answering fewer than half of them correctly. The evidence suggests that the system's performance on these difficult cases is not significantly different when using different reasoning strategies.
The study's findings cannot be applied to other artificial intelligence systems, languages other than English, or medical questions not focused on the United States.

Incorrect medical answers from the artificial intelligence system were much more likely to contain flawed reasoning than correct answers. This suggests that the explanation provided by the system offers useful clues about whether the final answer can be trusted, though it does not guarantee accuracy.

The newer version of the artificial intelligence tool can mimic the way doctors think through a case, but it cannot actually use that thinking process to improve its accuracy the way a human doctor would. This means the tool is not yet reliable for making final medical decisions on its own.

Because the tool explains its reasoning, doctors can check if the logic and facts are correct to help decide if the answer is trustworthy. However, this explanation does not guarantee the answer is right, as the tool can still make unpredictable errors in its thinking.
The study found that asking the artificial intelligence system to use a specific medical reasoning method did not make its answers more accurate than using its standard reasoning method.

Experts checked the explanations provided by the artificial intelligence system while pretending they did not know the correct answer, to see if the logic was flawed in the same way a doctor might encounter it.
Two internal medicine doctors checked the first hundred explanations provided by the advanced language model to ensure the medical logic and accuracy were appropriate.
The evidence does not show that using a differential diagnosis approach helps the older language model answer medical questions correctly, as its performance was lower than the standard method.

The evidence does not show that using a differential diagnosis approach improves the advanced language model's ability to answer medical questions correctly, as its performance was not reliably different from the standard method.

People often have difficulty understanding their symptoms and choosing the right doctor, while medical professionals struggle to make quick and accurate diagnoses due to the complexity of patient information. This difficulty can lead to delays or mistakes in care, especially in busy emergency settings.

New computer tools may help patients understand their likely conditions and which specialists to see, and they may also assist doctors in making better decisions. This could lead to better health outcomes and a smoother experience for patients, though the tools are not yet proven to replace professional judgment.

In emergency rooms, the fast pace of work can lead to mistakes in how quickly patients are seen, which can result in poorer care for those who need it most. New computer programs show promise in helping doctors sort patients by how serious their condition is, which could reduce waiting times and improve the quality of care.

Mistakes in sorting patients can happen in two ways: either a sick person is not seen quickly enough, or a less urgent case takes up space meant for someone more critical. Both types of errors hurt patients and waste limited medical resources.

Computer programs might help fix these sorting mistakes, which would lead to better use of medical resources and better outcomes for patients. These tools could also help people understand their own symptoms and decide which doctor to see, though their use in real, unpredictable medical situations is still being studied.

Using a private collection of emergency department records helps ensure that the artificial intelligence systems being tested have not already learned the answers from public data, making the evaluation more reliable.

Adding a system that pulls specific medical facts from a large library of research papers helps the artificial intelligence provide more accurate and informed answers while reducing the chance of it making things up.

Doctors in busy emergency rooms often face unclear symptoms and incomplete information, forcing them to rely on their own judgment rather than choosing from a simple list of options. The study found that computer programs can help doctors make these complex decisions, but the technology is still being developed and is not yet fully ready for real-world use.

The research tested how well computer programs could predict the urgency of a patient's condition, the correct medical specialist to see, and the likely diagnosis based on symptoms and vital signs. The findings suggest these tools could help streamline care for both doctors and patients, though they are still in the process of being improved.

The study compares how well an artificial intelligence system helps with medical decisions for two different groups: people at home who only describe their symptoms, and people in emergency rooms where basic health measurements are also available.

The researchers acknowledge that this system cannot provide a final diagnosis on its own because it lacks access to physical exams and lab tests, but it aims to mimic the early decision-making process for both home users and emergency room patients.

The study tested whether artificial intelligence could help emergency room staff decide how urgently a patient needs care, either by listening to a patient's symptoms or by reviewing their medical records.

The researchers judged the system's performance by checking if its urgency rating matched the official rating or was only slightly higher, a method chosen to avoid the risk of delaying critical care while preventing the system from being overwhelmed by overly cautious ratings.

Artificial intelligence tools are better at sorting patients into the right level of care when they have access to detailed health measurements rather than just symptoms. These tools are confident that they can tell the difference between life-threatening emergencies and less urgent situations, even if they sometimes struggle to pick the exact severity level for the most critical or least serious cases.
Identifying the correct medical specialist for a patient is essential for ensuring they receive effective and timely treatment while reducing healthcare costs by avoiding unnecessary referrals.

The study aimed to determine if artificial intelligence tools can help identify which medical specialist a patient should see, but the available data did not contain exact information on which specialist primary care doctors would actually consult.

To create a standard for comparison, an artificial intelligence tool was used to predict the most likely specialist for each patient diagnosis, and four medical professionals reviewed a portion of these predictions to check if they were appropriate.

The differences in how well the artificial intelligence systems guessed the correct medical department were very small, meaning all systems performed similarly for both regular users and medical professionals.

Adding basic health measurements to the information provided to the systems did not significantly improve their ability to predict the correct medical department, because the final diagnosis often depends on tests and observations that happen later in the patient's care.

The evidence shows small differences in how well different artificial intelligence models predict patient diagnoses, with all models performing better when the goal was to identify at least one correct diagnosis rather than the exact one. This finding suggests that these tools are more reliable at suggesting a possible condition than pinpointing the single correct one.

Providing the artificial intelligence with specific patient data improves its ability to interpret vital signs and make diagnostic decisions, particularly in clinical settings. However, early diagnosis remains difficult in fast-paced emergency rooms because many crucial details about a patient's condition are not yet available upon arrival.

The research team found that different artificial intelligence systems often agree on their predictions, which suggests their answers are generally reliable. However, because the systems make different mistakes on different cases, combining their strengths could significantly reduce the chance of a wrong diagnosis.

To check if the suggested medical departments were appropriate, four medical experts independently reviewed a portion of the results. The experts rated each suggestion as correct, partially correct, reasonable but not ideal, or incorrect to ensure the recommendations were trustworthy.

When checking if an artificial intelligence system's medical diagnosis matches a doctor's opinion, the system usually agrees with at least one doctor in most cases. This suggests the system can be a helpful partner in everyday clinical decisions where one expert's agreement is enough.

However, when the system's diagnosis must match the opinion of every doctor involved, the system is much less likely to be correct. This shows that it is difficult for the system to reach the kind of full agreement required in serious medical team discussions.

Clinicians generally found that the artificial intelligence system's suggestions for medical specialties were accurate or acceptable in almost all cases, with very few errors. However, some doctors judged the results more strictly than others, showing that human opinions on the quality of these suggestions can vary based on individual experience.

The artificial intelligence system is reliable for suggesting medical specialties, but doctors should still review its recommendations for complex medical situations. The system's output was found to align closely with what clinicians expected, though individual doctors sometimes disagreed on how well the system performed.

To ensure the artificial intelligence system can be trusted for medical decisions, researchers checked how well its predictions matched the judgments of human doctors. Four doctors independently reviewed the system's diagnosis suggestions to see if they agreed with the correct medical answers.

Artificial intelligence tools perform well when working alongside human doctors in flexible clinical situations, but they struggle to match the exact judgment of experts when complete agreement is required.
Different doctors often disagree with one another on medical assessments due to varying levels of experience and perspective, which makes it difficult to achieve a single unified conclusion.
These artificial intelligence systems can serve as helpful complementary tools in group discussions among medical specialists, where diverse viewpoints can improve the quality of medical decisions.

The study examined how well artificial intelligence models could support medical decisions by testing them on real-world patient cases to predict diagnoses, recommend specialists, and determine the urgency of care.

Artificial intelligence systems currently struggle to accurately determine the severity of a patient's condition, often making errors in both directions. This means the systems are not yet reliable enough to independently decide how urgent a patient's care needs are.

The evidence suggests that using written medical notes to predict patient severity may be biased because these notes are created after the initial assessment. Ideally, the systems would use real-time recordings of the first contact with medical staff, but this data is not available.

The difficulty these systems have in assigning correct severity levels highlights their current limitations in handling complex medical judgments on their own. Despite these flaws, the results still provide a useful measure of the overall quality and potential of these tools for future clinical assistance.

Artificial intelligence tools that can check answers against trusted outside sources are better at reducing the risk of making up incorrect medical facts than tools that rely only on their own internal knowledge. This extra checking step is important in healthcare settings where getting the details right is critical for patient safety.

The benefit of using outside research sources varies depending on the specific medical task, such as determining how urgent care is or identifying a disease. These tools perform best when the current scientific literature clearly connects the patient's physical measurements to the specific decision being made.

While checking against outside research helps identify the correct category for a patient's condition, it does not always help the system predict whether the condition is more or less severe than another. This is because research materials rarely provide guidance on ranking the relative severity of different cases.

The fact that different artificial intelligence systems do not always agree on their predictions suggests they could be combined to improve results by using the strengths of each system in different situations.

When doctors reviewed the predictions made by the artificial intelligence, their assessments varied based on individual judgment and experience, showing that reaching full agreement in medical decisions is complex.

Artificial intelligence systems cannot replace doctors in making complex medical decisions on their own, but they can help doctors by offering useful information and insights. These systems are better suited for supporting inexperienced doctors, helping patients understand their conditions, or performing basic safety checks.

For the study, information was gathered from patients in two different ways: from the patient describing their own symptoms and basic details, or from a doctor recording vital signs like temperature and heart rate upon arrival at the emergency department.

Artificial intelligence tools could help people at home understand how serious their symptoms are and which medical specialist to see, allowing them to make better choices about their care. However, using these tools for medical decisions is considered high-risk by regulators, meaning they would need to be thoroughly tested and constantly monitored before being used in clinics.

Doctors might start using publicly available artificial intelligence tools as helpers in their daily work without official approval, making it crucial to openly test how well these tools perform on medical tasks. This open testing is important for both medical professionals and the general public to ensure the tools are reliable.

A system that combines a search tool with an artificial intelligence model helps reduce the chance of the model giving false or misleading answers, making the information it provides more reliable and factual for people using it.

The system breaks down a patient's question into smaller parts to find the most relevant medical information from a large collection of research summaries. It then uses this information to create an answer and lists the specific research sources used so people can check the details themselves.

The system repeatedly checks its own answers to find any missing or incorrect information and improves the response before providing it to the user. This process aims to make the final answer more accurate and better aligned with the original question.

Doctors sometimes assign a higher urgency level to a patient than strictly necessary to be safe, which means a system can be considered correct if it predicts a slightly higher urgency level than the actual one, as long as it does not predict a lower one.

A system for recommending medical specialists was tested in two ways: one for regular people describing their symptoms, and another for doctors who also have access to the patient's basic health measurements.

The study used a large collection of hospital records that accurately represent patient information at the start of emergency care, providing a clear view of early clinical decisions. The evidence is considered reliable because the records match the actual patient data from that time.

The researchers designed the test to mimic a real clinic where a doctor would only use the first answer from the computer system. This approach shows how useful the system is in practice but does not prove it would be better if given multiple chances to answer.

The computer system was tested using a secure connection to protect patient privacy, which reduces the chance that the system had seen the data before. This makes the results more trustworthy, though it does not confirm the system's accuracy on new, unseen data.

The system is designed to help primary care doctors decide which medical expert to consult for a patient's symptoms, but it cannot confirm if a consultation is actually required because the available records lack that specific information.

Because patients often have multiple health conditions at once, the tool suggests the three most likely medical experts rather than just one, which helps reduce the risk of focusing on a single issue and gives doctors and patients more options to consider.
The tool is intended to provide helpful insights to support medical decisions, but the final choice of treatment or referral is always made by the doctor using their own professional judgment.

To ensure the suggested diagnoses were relevant to the patient's immediate visit, the study only included cases where the patient stayed in the hospital for less than one day, preventing the inclusion of conditions that might develop later during a longer stay.

The study used an artificial intelligence system to check if a predicted illness name had the same meaning or was closely related to the actual illness listed in a patient's medical records. This approach was chosen because simple text comparisons might miss cases where the same condition is described using different words.

Previous research shows that artificial intelligence systems can judge tasks in a way that closely matches human opinions, which supports their use for comparing medical diagnoses. This means the automated checking of illness names is considered a reliable method for this type of evaluation.
The study confirmed that all hospital stays were less than one day long to prevent including medical conditions that might develop later during a longer stay.
A computer system was used to check if the predicted medical conditions matched the actual ones, allowing for differences in wording while keeping the comparison fair.
Four medical professionals reviewed a portion of the data to compare the predicted conditions against the actual ones.

The evaluation for predicting the correct medical specialty only counted a prediction as correct if it exactly matched the actual list of specialists, even if other predicted specialists might also be relevant.
The research notes that a single medical condition can sometimes be managed by multiple specialists, a limitation the team plans to address in future work.
A second, simpler evaluation method considered a prediction successful if at least one of the predicted medical specialties matched the actual list of specialists for the patient.

Doctors from hospitals in Italy, Germany, and the United States independently checked the computer's answers to make sure the results were fair and objective. Each doctor reviewed a specific set of patient cases to ensure that different experts could agree on the quality of the predictions.

The doctors judged whether the computer correctly identified the right medical field for a patient's illness. They labeled each answer as correct, partially correct, reasonable but not perfect, or completely wrong based on how well it matched what a human expert would choose.

The doctors compared the computer's guessed illnesses against the confirmed diagnoses to see if the computer was right. They categorized each guess as an exact match, a different way of saying the same illness, a related but different condition, or a completely unrelated error.

The researchers used a type of artificial intelligence to check if its own medical predictions were correct, but they specifically avoided letting it compare different models against each other to prevent unfair bias. This approach was designed to make the checking process as objective as possible.

Although the automated checking method shows promise, it is not yet fully proven to be reliable or easy to understand in real hospital settings, so more work is needed to ensure it is safe for patients. To address this uncertainty, four medical experts from different hospitals reviewed a portion of the results to verify the accuracy of the system.

Four experienced doctors from different countries were asked to review how well the artificial intelligence system predicted medical specialties and diagnoses. These doctors had varied backgrounds and years of experience to provide a wide range of professional perspectives on the system's performance.

Artificial intelligence tools can act as a helpful and affordable second opinion for doctors, saving time while supporting medical decisions. The evidence suggests these tools are reliable enough to assist in this role, though the study does not prove they can replace human judgment entirely.

Different versions of the same artificial intelligence system often agree with each other when making medical predictions, suggesting the results are consistent. However, this does not show that the predictions are always correct, only that the system is stable in its outputs.

The study's main result might appear stronger than it truly is because the exact setup was not clearly documented, meaning we cannot fully trust the findings yet. This does not mean the medical A.I. technology is useless, but it does mean more proof is needed before relying on it for real decisions.

The comparison between the two groups of answers may be unreliable because the difference in error rates was not confirmed to be real rather than just random chance. Without clear proof that the gap is meaningful, the claim that incorrect answers contain significantly more logical errors does not hold up.

The medical A.I. model may have been tuned to satisfy the specific grading criteria rather than to improve its actual medical reasoning, which invalidates the comparison. This design flaw means the model's performance reflects its ability to match the evaluators' wording rather than its ability to diagnose correctly.

The reported improvement in accuracy might just be statistical noise if the confidence intervals overlap with the baseline error rate. This means the narrative of a robust improvement collapses, leaving us with a model that is merely consistent in its outputs rather than clinically better at diagnosing patients.

Computer models of a person's health can show how that specific person might react to a treatment, but these tools are still new and not fully proven. The current computer methods often struggle to explain their reasoning or handle incomplete information, and most only predict a single moment in the future rather than the person's long-term health path.

Newer computer programs designed to predict a patient's future health are mostly tested on short-term predictions rather than the long-term changes a person experiences over time. These programs also do not yet use the broad knowledge built into other advanced language systems, so they may not fully capture the complexity of a patient's situation.

A new computer system can create a virtual version of a patient to predict how their health will change over time. This tool uses a patient's medical history to help doctors choose treatments and monitor health without needing to fill in missing data.

The new prediction system performed better than current standard computer models when tested on patients with lung cancer, Alzheimer's disease, and those in intensive care. It also provided explanations for its predictions that people can understand, though the study did not test if this improves actual patient outcomes.

Virtual patient models can simulate how a specific person might respond to different medical treatments in real time. These models use a person's long-term medical history to make detailed predictions about their future health.

The new computer tool can predict how a patient's health will change over time, including for conditions like severe illness in the hospital, lung cancer, and Alzheimer's disease. It can also make predictions about health measures it has never seen before without needing extra training.

The computer tool was tested on records from patients with severe hospital illnesses, lung cancer, and Alzheimer's disease to see how well it predicts health changes over short, medium, and long periods. The researchers used these different groups of patients to check if the tool works well when there are many or few records available to learn from.

A new forecasting tool provided more accurate predictions of how patients' health would change over time compared to existing methods, which could help doctors monitor conditions and intervene sooner. The evidence is strong because the tool was tested on patients it had never seen before and outperformed fourteen other established prediction methods.

The new forecasting tool was compared against fourteen other prediction methods, ranging from simple techniques to advanced artificial intelligence systems, to verify its accuracy. The tool was also compared to two other large language models to understand the specific benefit of its specialized medical training.

The new forecasting tool produced the most accurate predictions for patient health metrics across three different medical conditions compared to all other tested methods. This result indicates the tool is currently the best at predicting future patient outcomes in these specific scenarios.

A new type of computer model can predict a patient's future health status without needing to be specifically trained on that patient's data first. This shows the model is very flexible and can apply its general knowledge to new situations.

Previous prediction methods often looked at different health measurements separately, which misses the connections between them. In real patient care, these measurements are linked by biological causes, so a better approach needs to look at all of a patient's health data at the same time.

The new system creates a digital copy of a patient using records from real-world medical visits and studies. These records contain valuable information about a patient's background, diagnoses, and test results, but they are often messy, incomplete, or inconsistent, which makes them difficult to use for building accurate models.
The model's predictions for a specific blood cell type were mostly accurate for most patients, but the largest errors came from a small group of people whose medical history was unusual.
The model successfully matched the overall pattern of health measurements across the group of patients, which is a necessary step for making predictions that are useful in a medical setting.

The new prediction tool is better than other existing tools at spotting general changes in blood test results for people with lung cancer, severe illness, or Alzheimer's disease. However, the evidence is not strong enough to say the tool can reliably predict rare or specific dangerous drops in blood counts.

The prediction tool is good at noticing common, mild changes in blood levels that doctors watch for in lung cancer patients, such as low red blood cell counts or signs of inflammation. It does not show that the tool can accurately predict rare, critical emergencies where blood counts drop dangerously low.

The prediction tool keeps the natural connections between different blood test results intact when it makes its forecasts. This means the tool's predictions for one test result stay logically consistent with its predictions for other test results over time.
The tool can still make useful predictions even when some patient information is missing or contains spelling errors, a problem that usually forces other methods to discard the data entirely.
The tool can explain its predictions by identifying which factors, such as the type of treatment or the patient's physical condition, most strongly influence the expected health outcomes.

Patients receiving certain types of cancer treatment, such as immunotherapy, generally maintain higher blood cell counts over time compared to those receiving chemotherapy, which tends to lower these counts.

The research found that a specific forecasting method was better at spotting important health events in patients than other standard methods, even though it was only trained to predict future trends. This suggests the tool can help identify when a patient is likely to experience a significant change in their condition.

The study suggests that artificial intelligence systems may work well for predicting patient health because they handle missing information in a way similar to how humans understand language. For example, just as a doctor might leave out a measurement if a patient looks healthy, these systems can interpret what is not said or recorded as meaningful information.

The study found that a simple method for training language models on patient records allows the creation of digital twins that mimic individual patients. This approach helps in selecting treatments and supporting clinical trials by accurately predicting future health events.

The evidence suggests that the model performs well when predicting health variables that are closely linked to the main conditions being studied. It may also capture meaningful relationships between specific blood markers in patients with lung cancer, though this is based on limited analysis rather than broad proof.

The model's predictions closely match the real-world patterns of patient data, indicating high confidence that the generated simulations reflect actual patient experiences. It also remains reliable even when the input data contains common issues like missing information or spelling errors.

A patient's recent level of physical ability and age are strong indicators of how their blood cell counts will change over time, and these predictions match what is seen in their actual medical records. This suggests the model's forecasts are reliable for understanding a patient's health trajectory.

The model can predict the future values of many different health measures that were not specifically used to train it, without needing any extra practice on those specific tests. This means the tool can provide useful forecasts for a wide range of patient data beyond its original focus.

Even though the model was not specifically trained on these extra health measures, it still made better predictions than a standard computer program for some of them. This success happened mainly for health measures that are closely related to the ones the model was originally trained on, showing it can connect similar types of medical data.

The medical prediction tool can explain the reasoning behind its forecasts, which helps doctors understand and trust the results. This ability may improve how clinicians use artificial intelligence in their daily work.

The prediction system can forecast health measures it was not specifically trained to predict, and it sometimes performs better than standard models on these new tasks. This shows the tool can adapt to new situations without needing extra training.

The system sometimes provides explanations that are not true, which is a serious concern for medical care. To address this, doctors must be trained to carefully review the system's output rather than trusting it completely.

The system tends to repeat unfair patterns found in its training data, which especially harms people from minority groups. Fixing this requires collecting much more diverse patient data and training the people who use the system.

The system often makes large errors because it generates many different possible future paths for a patient and averages them together, which can hide important details. A better method is needed to pick the most realistic path, possibly by having a human expert choose the best one.

The researchers believe that improved computer models of individual patients will eventually help doctors choose the best treatments and monitor patients more effectively. They envision these models becoming a standard part of healthcare systems.

The new method uses general computer language programs that have been adjusted with medical records to predict future health measurements for patients. This approach was tested on records from people with lung cancer, those in critical care, and people with Alzheimer's disease.

For the lung cancer study, the researchers used a large collection of medical records from about 280 cancer clinics across the United States. The records were processed to remove personal identifying information to protect patient privacy.

The computer model showed strong ability to predict common health changes like anemia and inflammation, but it struggled to accurately forecast rare and sudden severe drops in blood counts. This means the tool is currently less reliable for catching critical, high-risk emergencies.

The researchers suggest the model might be picking up on hidden medical patterns, such as the relationship between certain blood proteins, but these are only early guesses that need thorough checking by doctors before they can be trusted.

The system currently has a limited number of health signs it can predict at once because of technical restrictions on how much information it can process. Future updates aim to fix this so the tool can handle more patient details and become useful for a wider range of medical situations.

The study measured how well the prediction model could identify if a health measurement was moving up or down over time. It checked if the model's predicted direction of change matched the actual direction seen in the patient's data.

The study used a large group of hospital records to test if a computer model could predict a patient's oxygen levels, breathing rate, and magnesium levels for the next day based on their first day in the intensive care unit. The researchers chose these specific health measures because they change quickly and are tracked for many patients.

The researchers also tested their model on a separate group of people with early memory loss to see if it could predict how their thinking and memory would change over two years. The model was trained to forecast the results of three standard memory tests based on the patients' starting scores.

The research team used a computer program to explain which health factors most strongly influenced its predictions about a patient's future condition. This program was also tested on predicting new health measures it had never been specifically trained to forecast.

The study used specific mathematical methods to measure how far off the computer program's predictions were from the actual health values recorded for patients. These methods provide an objective way to judge the accuracy of the predictions.

The medical information tool is not reliable enough to replace your regular doctor because it cannot be verified whether its mistakes come from broken data processing or a lack of true medical knowledge. You should continue using your standard healthcare provider for health decisions rather than relying on this untested system.

The evidence for the diagnostic tool's competence is too uncertain to trust because the wide range of possible error rates means we cannot distinguish between a flawed data setup and a genuinely weak model. This uncertainty means the claim that the tool improves diagnostic accuracy is not supported by the available data.

The computer system may not be learning how the body actually functions, but instead just guessing based on general patient details like age or how sick they appear to be. This means the tool's accuracy claims are effectively null because it is not detecting specific physiological changes.

The medical assessment tool currently acts only as an unverified helper and cannot replace a doctor's judgment because there is no stable standard to prove it is correctly identifying health signals. This means the tool does not show that a patient's specific condition has been definitively confirmed or ruled out, nor does it prove the doctor's diagnosis is wrong.
